pullquote: Fast from the world, not from food. Keep sabbath in your soul, not on a calendar.
core_message: The real fast is withdrawal from the world's grip, and the real sabbath is inner rest in the Father.

primary.jesus_words: <Jesus said,> "If you do not fast as regards the world, you will not find the kingdom. If you do not observe the Sabbath as a Sabbath, you will not see the father."

context: Two commands that sound external and turn out to be entirely internal. If you do not fast as regards the world, you will not find the kingdom. Fasting here is not skipping meals. It is disengaging from the values, appetites, and anxieties that the world runs on — status, accumulation, revenge, control. The Ebionim community lived this literally, holding possessions in common, refusing the imperial economy. Fasting from the world means loosening its hooks in you.

title: Drunk and Blind
pullquote: He found humanity intoxicated — full of everything except the thirst that would have led them home.
core_message: Humanity is drunk on distraction and empty of the thirst that would awaken us to the kingdom.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "I took my place in the midst of the world, and I appeared to them in flesh. I found all of them intoxicated; I found none of them thirsty. And my soul became afflicted for the sons of men, because they are blind in their hearts and do not have sight; for empty they came into the world, and empty too they seek to leave the world. But for the moment they are intoxicated. When they shake off their wine, then they will repent."

context: This is one of the most sober diagnoses of the human condition in any sayings tradition. Jesus takes his place in the midst of the world. He appears in flesh. And what does he find. Everyone intoxicated. Not one of them thirsty. His soul is grieved for them — they are blind in their hearts. They came into the world empty and they will leave the world empty, having filled the space in between with wine that dulls them into unconsciousness.

title: Great Wealth in Poverty
pullquote: That the infinite would make its home in a body — this is the wonder of wonders.
core_message: The astonishing thing is not that flesh exists, but that infinite spirit chose to dwell in it.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "If the flesh came into being because of spirit, it is a wonder. But if spirit came into being because of the body, it is a wonder of wonders. Indeed, I am amazed at how this great wealth has made its home in this poverty."

context: Jesus muses aloud like a philosopher. If flesh came into being because of spirit, that would be a wonder — matter emerging from mind, the physical born of the invisible. But if spirit came into being because of the body, that would be a wonder of wonders — the reverse would be almost unthinkable. He is not settling the question. He is holding up the mystery. Then the punchline: I am amazed at how this great wealth has made its home in this poverty.

title: Disrobe Without Shame
pullquote: Strip off the shame you were taught. Tread on it like a child. Then you'll see.
core_message: You will see the living one when you shed the shame that hides your true self.

primary.jesus_words: His disciples said, "When will you become revealed to us and when shall we see you?" Jesus said, "When you disrobe without being ashamed and take up your garments and place them under your feet like little children and tread on them, then will you see the son of the living one, and you will not be afraid"

context: The disciples ask when Jesus will be revealed to them. His answer is not about the timing of his return. It is about what has to happen in them before they can see. Disrobe without being ashamed. Take up your garments and tread on them like children. Then you will see the son of the living one, and you will not be afraid.

title: Grapevine Outside the Father
pullquote: Anything not rooted in the source will not last. Nothing you build outside the Father survives.
core_message: Whatever grows apart from the source is unsound and will not endure.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "A grapevine has been planted outside of the father, but being unsound, it will be pulled up by its roots and destroyed."

context: The image is agricultural and unambiguous. A grapevine planted outside the Father is unsound. It will be pulled up by its roots and destroyed. Not because God is destructive. Because life without connection to the source cannot sustain itself. The synoptics carry a parallel in the parable of the wheat and the weeds, and John 15 develops the same image at length — I am the vine, you are the branches, apart from me you can do nothing.

title: Become Passers-By
pullquote: Two words. The whole path in miniature. Don't grip. Don't cling. Pass by.
core_message: Live like someone passing through — attached to nothing, free to keep moving toward the source.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Become passers-by."

context: Two words in the original Coptic. *Šōpe ĕtĕtnparage*. Become passers-by. It is the shortest saying in Thomas and one of the most demanding. Jesus is not telling his disciples to be indifferent or emotionally distant. He is telling them not to grip. Do not build monuments to yourself. Do not accumulate. Do not settle into the world as if it were your permanent home. Pass through.

title: Love the Tree or Its Fruit
pullquote: You cannot love the fruit and hate the tree. Or love the tree and hate its fruit. Both go together.
core_message: You cannot separate a teaching from the life that produces it — or love the life and reject the teaching.

primary.jesus_words: His disciples said to him, "Who are you, that you should say these things to us?" <Jesus said to them,> "You do not realize who I am from what I say to you, but you have become like the Jews, for they (either) love the tree and hate its fruit (or) love the fruit and hate the tree."

context: The disciples ask a strange question — who are you, that you should say these things to us. Jesus's answer is sharper than expected. You do not know me from what I say to you. You have become like those who love the tree and hate its fruit, or love the fruit and hate the tree. This is a diagnosis of religious inconsistency. People want the teaching without the teacher, or the teacher as a personality without the teaching that made him what he is. Neither works.

title: Two at Peace
pullquote: When two people in one house make peace, mountains move. That's not metaphor. That's the mechanism.
core_message: Reconciliation between two people releases power sufficient to move what looks immovable.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "If two make peace with each other in this one house, they will say to the mountain, 'Move Away,' and it will move away."

context: The mountain-moving saying appears in three variations across the tradition. Matthew 17:20 attributes the power to faith the size of a mustard seed. Matthew 21:21 ties it to faith without doubt. Thomas 48 makes it something different and, if you sit with it, more practical. Two people. One house. If they make peace with each other — the mountain moves.

title: The Solitary Will Find It
pullquote: You came from the kingdom. You'll return to it. And the ones who become whole find it first.
core_message: The undivided self recognizes its origin in the kingdom and its return to it.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Blessed are the solitary and elect, for you will find the kingdom. For you are from it, and to it you will return."

context: Blessed are the solitary and elect, for you will find the kingdom. Solitary here does not mean lonely or antisocial. The Coptic word behind it, *monachos*, means single, unified, whole — the same root behind Thomas 22's making the two into one. The solitary are the ones who have integrated the divided self, who no longer live pulled between competing loyalties, who have become simple in the deep sense of the word.

title: Children of the Light
pullquote: Where did you come from? The light. Who are you? Its children. What is the sign? Movement and repose.
core_message: Your true identity is child of the light — and its signature in you is both action and rest.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "If they say to you, 'Where did you come from?', say to them, 'We came from the light, the place where the light came into being on its own accord and established itself and became manifest through their image.' If they say to you, 'Is it you?', say, 'We are its children, we are the elect of the living father.' If they ask you, 'What is the sign of your father in you?', say to them, 'It is movement and repose.'"

context: This is a catechism of the awakened. When the world challenges you, here is what to say. Where did you come from? From the light, the place where the light came into being on its own accord, established itself, and became manifest through their image. Notice the language — self-arising light. Not created light. The source. And that source made itself visible in image — the *imago dei* of Genesis, the divine likeness stamped on humanity.

title: It Has Already Come
pullquote: You keep looking forward to the new world. It's already here. You just aren't recognizing it.
core_message: What most people wait for as future has already arrived — the failure is recognition, not timing.

primary.jesus_words: His disciples said to him, "When will the repose of the dead come about, and when will the new world come?" He said to them, "What you look forward to has already come, but you do not recognize it."

context: The disciples ask when the rest of the dead will come and when the new world will begin. Jesus's answer is one of the clearest statements of realized eschatology in any tradition. What you look forward to has already come, but you do not recognize it. This is not a promise for later. It is a diagnosis of now. The kingdom, the new creation, the resurrection life, the age to come — it is already present, and the problem is your eyes.

title: The Living Among You
pullquote: Twenty-four prophets spoke of him. And they're still only talking about the dead one you're missing right now.
core_message: Reverence for past prophets is worthless if you cannot recognize the living presence right in front of you.

primary.jesus_words: His disciples said to him, "Twenty-four prophets spoke in Israel, and all of them spoke in you." He said to them, "You have omitted the one living in your presence and have spoken (only) of the dead."

context: The disciples try to compliment Jesus by placing him in the line of the twenty-four prophets of Israel — the traditional count of the Hebrew Bible's prophetic books. All of them spoke of you. Jesus is not flattered. You have omitted the one living in your presence and have spoken only of the dead. It is a sharp corrective. Do not bury me under a stack of ancestors. Notice me now.

title: Circumcision in Spirit
pullquote: If circumcision mattered, babies would arrive that way. What matters is the circumcision of the heart.
core_message: External religious markers count for nothing; only the inward circumcision of the heart is real.

primary.jesus_words: His disciples said to him, "Is circumcision beneficial or not?" He said to them, "If it were beneficial, their father would beget them already circumcised from their mother. Rather, the true circumcision in spirit has become completely profitable."

context: The disciples ask a live question of the first century — is circumcision beneficial. Jesus's answer is deadpan and devastating. If it were beneficial, their father would beget them already circumcised from their mother. The argument from design cuts the ritual off at the knees. God did not include it in the equipment. Rather, the true circumcision in spirit has become completely profitable.

title: The World is a Corpse
pullquote: See the world for what it is and you are no longer owned by it. Understanding is the first act of freedom.
core_message: Once you truly understand the world of appearances, you see it is lifeless, and that seeing lifts you above it.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Whoever has come to understand the world has found (only) a corpse, and whoever has found a corpse is superior to the world."

context: This is a Thomas saying with the bite of Ecclesiastes. Once you look through the world of power, status, and possession, you find nothing living there — just a shell that outlives whoever chased it. Solomon called it *hevel* — vapor, breath. Thomas calls it a corpse. Same insight. The world people are scrambling to own is already dead; only the scramble keeps it looking alive. To understand this is to stop feeding the illusion.

title: Blessed is the One Who Has Suffered
pullquote: Suffering is not the point. What you find on the other side of it is.
core_message: Suffering that leads to real life is a blessing, because it burns away what was never you to begin with.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Blessed is the man who has suffered and found life."

context: This is a Thomas beatitude that never made it into Matthew's collection, but it belongs alongside them. Jesus is not glorifying pain — he is naming what suffering can do when it is received rather than resisted. It strips away the false self. It ends the illusion that the ego can control outcomes. When the constructed identity collapses under weight it cannot carry, what remains is the life that was underneath the whole time. That is why the saying blesses the one who *has* suffered — past tense — and found life. The finding is the point.

title: While You Are Alive
pullquote: You will not find after death what you refused to seek while living. The kingdom has a threshold, and it is here.
core_message: Seek the living presence of God now while you are able, because the search cannot be deferred to after you die.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Take heed of the living one while you are alive, lest you die and seek to see him and be unable to do so."

context: This is one of Thomas's most sober sayings. Jesus is not threatening hell. He is stating a fact about consciousness. The window for waking up is this life. Whatever capacity you build now for perceiving the living one — the presence of God within and around you — is the capacity you carry forward. Whatever you fail to cultivate is not automatically handed to you later. The search has to happen while there is still someone here to search.

title: Do Not Become a Corpse
pullquote: Whatever you feed on, you become. Find your rest in the living, or you will be eaten by what you served.
core_message: Live in an inner state of repose grounded in the living God, or you become spiritually dead and consumed by the world.

primary.jesus_words: <They saw> a Samaritan carrying a lamb on his way to Judea. He said to his disciples, "That man is round about the lamb." They said to him, "So that he may kill it and eat it." He said to them, "While it is alive, he will not eat it, but only when he has killed it and it has become a corpse." They said to him, "He cannot do so otherwise." He said to them, "You too, look for a place for yourself within repose, lest you become a corpse and be eaten."

context: The disciples watch a Samaritan carry a lamb toward Judea, and they know the lamb will end up on a plate. Jesus turns it into a mirror. The lamb has to die to be eaten — and Jesus is telling his followers not to die that same death. Do not become a corpse. Do not let yourself go so cold, so cut off from the living center, that the world can swallow you whole. Find your place within *repose* — the still, alive presence of God — while there is still time to find it.

title: Knowing the All
pullquote: If you have touched the fullness of God and still feel empty, you have not touched it at all.
core_message: Anyone who claims to know the whole and still feels lacking has not actually known it.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "If one who knows the all still feels a personal deficiency, he is completely deficient."

context: This saying is a diagnostic. Jesus is not shaming the deficient — he is describing what real awakening produces. When you have actually perceived the fullness of God (the *pleroma*, the all, what Paul in a rare moment of clarity called the fullness in whom you are complete), you cannot simultaneously feel a personal lack. The two states are mutually exclusive. So if the sense of deficiency is still driving you — needing to be seen, needing more, needing to be right — the knowing has not landed. It is still theoretical.

title: Bring It Forth
pullquote: The kingdom is not something you download from outside. It is something you deliver from inside — or it kills you.
core_message: What lives within you must be brought out to save you, and what is not there cannot save you at all.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "That which you have will save you if you bring it forth from yourselves. That which you do not have within you will kill you if you do not have it within you."

context: This is one of Thomas's sharpest lines. There is no external rescue. Whatever will save you has to already be in you — and it has to be brought forth, expressed, lived, given away. Hidden, it does nothing. Undeveloped, it does nothing. The parable of the talents makes the same point (Mt 25:14-30) — the servant who buried his gift is the one who lost everything. The kingdom does not arrive from the sky. It rises from the inside and out into the world through your life. That is the whole shape of Jesus's way.

title: Nothing in the Cistern
pullquote: A crowd around the trough. A dry well underneath. Presence without depth is the perennial danger.
core_message: Many gather around the source, but the source itself has run dry when there is nothing living underneath.

primary.jesus_words: He said, "O Lord, there are many around the drinking trough, but there is nothing in the cistern."

context: This little saying reads like a lament, spoken to the Lord by someone in the community — perhaps a disciple, perhaps Jesus himself. Many are drawn to the outward form of the teaching. Few have done the interior work that fills the cistern in the first place. Crowds around a trough with no water underneath is a picture of religion without transformation. It is a picture of Jesus's own following at points in his ministry — thousands gathered for bread and healing, hundreds by the end, eleven at the cross.

title: Found the Body
pullquote: Understand the world and you find only a body. Find the body and you already stand above it.
core_message: Recognizing the world for what it materially is puts you above being ruled by it.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "He who has recognized the world has found the body, but he who has found the body is superior to the world."

context: Thomas 80 is a near-twin of Thomas 56 — the same insight in slightly different key. Where 56 says *corpse*, 80 says *body*. Both are contrasting the world of matter and appearance with the awareness that perceives it. When you have actually recognized the world — its impermanence, its emptiness of the deep life you were looking for — you have found the body. And whoever has found the body is superior to it. Perception itself is the liberation.

title: Renounce Power
pullquote: If you have grown rich, take the throne. If you have taken the throne, put it down. Kingdom logic runs upside-down.
core_message: Real spiritual authority comes to those who let go of the power the world hands them.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Let him who has grown rich be king, and let him who possesses power renounce it."

context: This is Thomas turning the world's operating system on its head. Let the rich one become king — sure, take the crown you have been chasing. But whoever actually holds power, renounce it. The saying is not endorsing wealth and rule. It is exposing them. If you climb the ladder all the way to the top, the only sane thing to do at the summit is to step off. The path of the world ends in a renunciation, or it ends in ruin. There is no third option.

title: The Light in the Image
pullquote: Everything visible is carrying a hidden light. The Father shows himself and hides himself in the same act.
core_message: The visible forms of the world contain a concealed divine light that reveals God even while veiling him.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "The images are manifest to man, but the light in them remains concealed in the image of the light of the father. He will become manifest, but his image will remain concealed by his light."

context: This is Thomas at its most contemplative. Images — every visible form, every face, every leaf — are manifest to us. But the light inside them, the light of the Father that gives them being, stays concealed inside the image. And when that light does become manifest, the image itself becomes the veil. God shows and hides in a single motion. This is how the presence works. You cannot look directly at the sun; you see it in what it lights up. You cannot look directly at God; you see God in what God is making right now.

title: The Images That Came Before You
pullquote: You rejoice at your reflection. Wait until you see the self that was before the reflection began.
core_message: The transient likeness you love is easy; the eternal image behind it will be harder to bear.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "When you see your likeness, you rejoice. But when you see your images which came into being before you, and which neither die not become manifest, how much you will have to bear!"

context: You look in the mirror and enjoy what you see — the face, the personality, the story of yourself you have curated. That likeness is comfortable. Jesus is pointing to something else. There is an image of you that came into being before you did — the eternal blueprint, the *imago Dei*, what Genesis 1:27 calls the image and likeness of God. That image does not die and does not become manifest in the ordinary way. To meet it is to meet what you actually are underneath the personality. And it will cost you.

title: Adam Was Not Worthy
pullquote: The first human had every advantage and still fell. You have something Adam did not — and you are meant to surpass him.
core_message: Adam had great power and wealth but was not worthy of the awakening now offered to Jesus's disciples.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Adam came into being from a great power and a great wealth, but he did not become worthy of you. For had he been worthy, he would not have experienced death."

context: This is a hard saying to hear at first. Adam — the archetype of humanity — came into being with every advantage. Great power. Great wealth. Made in the image, walking with God in the garden. And still he did not become worthy of what Jesus is offering his disciples. If he had been worthy, he would not have experienced death. The saying is not condemning Adam personally. It is naming the whole condition Jesus came to answer. The first human fell asleep. The second human — the *bar enasha*, the human one — came to wake everyone up.

title: Body Depending on Body
pullquote: When flesh clings to flesh and soul clings to both, everything is upside-down. Rest in what does not decay.
core_message: A life whose body depends on other bodies and whose soul depends on those bodies is a life in bondage.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Wretched is the body that is dependant upon a body, and wretched is the soul that is dependent on these two."

context: The saying is stacked. A body that depends on another body — needing another person to complete it, to define it, to prop it up — is already in trouble. A soul that depends on those two dependent bodies is in even worse trouble. Jesus is describing the whole chain of misplaced dependency that runs modern life: needing the other person, needing their approval, and staking your inner state on that dependency. Wretched. Not because bodies are evil, but because bodies cannot bear the weight of being your source.

title: Give What You Have
pullquote: The angels and prophets bring you what is already yours. Pass it on and ask when what belongs to them will be claimed.
core_message: Give away what you already possess spiritually, and expect that what is yours to receive will find you.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "The angels and the prophets will come to you and give to you those things you (already) have. And you too, give them those things which you have, and say to yourselves, 'When will they come and take what is theirs?'"

context: This is an odd, luminous saying. Angels and prophets come and give you things you already have — the truth was in you before they arrived; they only reflect it back and confirm it. That is the whole function of a genuine teacher, and it is what Jesus said about himself elsewhere: the kingdom is within you (Lk 17:21). The teacher does not implant the kingdom. The teacher points you to what is already there. So when the angels and prophets deliver, they are giving you your own.

title: The Empty Jar
pullquote: The kingdom does not always slip away with a bang. Sometimes it just leaks out behind you while you walk.
core_message: The kingdom can be lost quietly through inattention, without any dramatic failure, until you arrive home and find nothing left.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "The kingdom of the father is like a certain woman who was carrying a jar full of meal. While she was walking on the road, still some distance from home, the handle of the jar broke and the meal emptied out behind her on the road. She did not realize it; she had noticed no accident. When she reached her house, she set the jar down and found it empty."

context: This is one of Thomas's most disturbing parables, and it belongs beside Jesus's other warnings about inattention. A woman walks home from the mill with a jar of meal. The handle breaks. Meal trickles out behind her the whole way home. She notices nothing. She sets the jar down. It is empty. That is the whole story. No enemy stole from her. No storm broke the jar. Her own inattention did the work. When she finally looked, everything was gone.

title: Testing the Sword
pullquote: Practice at home what you intend to do in the world. The kingdom is built the same way.
core_message: The kingdom is like someone who first tests his capacity privately before acting on it publicly.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "The kingdom of the father is like a certain man who wanted to kill a powerful man. In his own house he drew his sword and stuck it into the wall in order to find out whether his hand could carry through. Then he slew the powerful man."

context: This is one of the strangest kingdom parables in any gospel, and it does not appear in the canon. A man wants to kill a powerful man. Before he tries, he stabs his sword into his own wall to see whether his hand can carry the blow through. It can. So he goes and does the deed. The violent frame is startling — but the kingdom principle underneath is one Jesus taught in gentler forms. Count the cost before you build the tower. Do not go to war without first sitting down to see if you can win (Lk 14:28-32).

title: Dog in the Manger
pullquote: They will not enter, and they will not let anyone else in either. That is the whole indictment.
core_message: The Pharisees block others from what they themselves refuse to receive.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Woe to the pharisees, for they are like a dog sleeping in the manger of oxen, for neither does he eat nor does he let the oxen eat."

context: This saying has close cousins in the canonical woes. Woe to you experts in the law, Jesus says in Luke 11:52, because you have taken away the key to knowledge — you did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering. Matthew 23:13 says the same: you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces; you neither enter yourselves nor let those enter who are trying to. Thomas 102 gives the picture in one homely image. A dog lies in the manger of the oxen. He is not going to eat the hay. He will not let the oxen eat it either. Pure obstruction with no benefit to anyone, including himself.

title: Son of a Harlot
pullquote: Know your true origin, and the world will insult you for it. The insult is the mark of the awakening.
core_message: Whoever knows the true source of their being will be slandered by a world that only recognizes worldly parentage.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "He who knows the father and the mother will be called the son of a harlot."

context: This is one of Thomas's cryptic sayings, and it takes some unfolding. In first-century Palestine, calling someone the *son of a harlot* was the gravest insult — an attack on legitimacy, honor, family name, standing in the community. Jesus says: whoever knows the true father and mother — the divine origin, the source beyond biological parentage — will get called exactly that. Because to know your true origin is to sit lightly to your worldly one, and a world that only understands worldly lineage cannot help but slander you for it.

title: Drink From My Mouth
pullquote: The teacher and the student become one. That is the whole point of a rabbi and a talmid.
core_message: Whoever fully receives Jesus's teaching becomes like him and receives revelation of what is hidden.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "He who will drink from my mouth will become like me. I myself shall become he, and the things that are hidden will be revealed to him."

context: This is the *talmid* relationship spelled out in one line. In the first-century rabbinic world, a disciple did not just learn the rabbi's ideas — the disciple *became* the rabbi. Same walk, same speech, same responses to trouble. Jesus said it plainly in Matthew 10:24-25 and Luke 6:40: it is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher. John 13:15 — I have given you an example. Thomas 108 says the same thing in more intimate language. Whoever drinks from my mouth — receives the teaching directly, without filter, without dilution — becomes like me. And *I myself shall become he*. The two collapse into one shared reality.

title: Renounce the World
pullquote: If you have found the world and grown rich in it, the next move is to let it go. Otherwise it owns you.
core_message: Whoever succeeds in the world's terms must then renounce the world to stay free.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Whoever finds the world and becomes rich, let him renounce the world."

context: This is Thomas 81 in slightly different wording, and it points to the same reality. You can succeed on the world's terms — accumulate, achieve, get everything you were told to want. And once you have, the only sane response is to let it go. Not because the world is evil, but because possession without renunciation reverses the ownership. What you clutch begins to clutch you. Jesus watched a rich young man discover this in real time (Mk 10:17-22). He had kept the commandments. He had done well. The one thing he lacked was the freedom to let go. And he walked away grieved.

title: Whoever Finds Himself
pullquote: Heaven and earth roll up in your presence when you know who you are. Find the self, transcend the world.
core_message: Whoever lives from the living source and finds their true self is beyond death and above the world.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "The heavens and the earth will be rolled up in your presence. And the one who lives from the living one will not see death." Does not Jesus say, "Whoever finds himself is superior to the world?"

context: This saying is two teachings stitched together. First — the heavens and the earth will be rolled up in your presence. Not a cosmic destruction from outside, but a shift in what you see. When you awaken, the whole system of appearances loses the ultimacy it seemed to have. It rolls up like a scroll (echoing Isaiah 34:4 and used again in Revelation 6:14 — but here re-cast interiorly). The one who lives from the living one will not see death. This is Jesus's core promise, in many keys — whoever keeps my word will never taste death (Jn 8:51-52); everyone living and believing in me shall never die (Jn 11:26); the kingdom is within (Lk 17:21).

title: Flesh and Soul
pullquote: Neither is meant to lean on the other. Both were meant to lean on God.
core_message: A flesh that leans on soul and a soul that leans on flesh are both in trouble — both were made to rest in God.

primary.jesus_words: Jesus said, "Woe to the flesh that depends on the soul; woe to the soul that depends on the flesh."

context: This paired *woe* is deceptively simple. Woe to the flesh that depends on the soul. Woe to the soul that depends on the flesh. Neither dependency works. If your body-life is trying to draw its meaning from your interior life, and your interior life is trying to draw its meaning from your body-life, the whole system collapses into itself. Both flesh and soul were made to rest in the Father — the *living one* Thomas keeps naming. Any other arrangement is bondage.

title: Mary Made Living Spirit
pullquote: Peter tries to exclude Mary. Jesus refuses. Whoever awakens the living spirit — man or woman — is in the kingdom.
core_message: Jesus defends Mary against Peter's exclusion and declares that every woman who awakens the living spirit within enters the kingdom.

primary.jesus_words: Simon Peter said to him, "Let Mary leave us, for women are not worthy of life." Jesus said, "I myself shall lead her in order to make her male, so that she too may become a living spirit resembling you males. For every woman who will make herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven." The Gospel According to Thomas

context: This is the most controversial saying in Thomas, and the most misread. Peter says let Mary leave us, for women are not worthy of life — a straight statement of the patriarchal assumption of the era. Jesus refuses. He says he himself will lead her, so that she too becomes a *living spirit* like the male disciples. In first-century language, *male* was code for the fully-realized human — active, awake, participating. *Female*, in this same rhetorical frame, meant the un-awakened, the receptive-only, the not-yet. Jesus is not erasing Mary. He is dignifying her. He is telling Peter that she has the same access to becoming a living spirit that any of them do. The saying is Jesus's refusal to let his community exclude women — a refusal consistent with everything the gospels report about him.

title: What Matter Cannot Hold
pullquote: Sin does not exist as a thing. It is what you make when you act against your true nature.
core_message: Every created form returns to its root, sin is not a substance but an action against nature, and inner contentment is the medicine.

primary.jesus_words: "Every nature, every form, every creature exists in and with each other, but they'll dissolve again into their own roots, because the nature of matter dissolves into its nature alone. Anyone who has ears to hear should hear! ... Sin doesn't exist, but you're the ones who make sin when you act in accordance with the nature of adultery, which is called 'sin.' That's why the Good came among you, up to the things of every nature in order to restore it within its root. ... That's why you get sick and die, because you love what tricks you. Anyone who can understand should understand! Matter gave birth to a passion that has no image because it came from what's contrary to nature. Then confusion arises in the whole body. That's why I told you to be content at heart. If you're discontented, find contentment in the presence of the various images of nature."

context: This is a rich teaching from the Savior in the Gospel of Mary — dialogue material recorded in the community around Mary Magdalene after the resurrection. The Savior begins with metaphysics. Every nature, every form, every creature holds together in mutual dependence and eventually dissolves back into its own root. Matter returns to matter. Nothing here is being demonized — this is simply how the material order works. Then the pivot that jumps off the page: *sin does not exist*. Not as a substance, not as a stain, not as a thing baked into you at birth. Sin is what you *make* when you act contrary to your true nature. It is a verb, not a noun. This is exactly the Jesus Way understanding of sin — harm you do, not a metaphysical debt you owe.

title: Peace Be With You
pullquote: The Son of Humanity is within you. Follow him. And do not build a new law where he refused to build one.
core_message: Jesus commissions the disciples with peace, tells them the kingdom is within, and forbids adding rules or laws beyond what he taught.

primary.jesus_words: "Peace be with you! Acquire my peace. Be careful not to let anyone mislead you by saying, 'Look over here!' or 'Look over there!' Because the Son of Humanity exists within you. Follow him! Those who seek him will find him. Go then and preach the gospel about the kingdom. Don't lay down any rules beyond what I've given you, nor make a law like the lawgiver, lest you be bound by it."

context: This is the Savior's parting instruction in the Gospel of Mary, and it is one of the most concentrated summaries of the Jesus Way anywhere in the early literature. Peace be with you. Acquire my peace — meaning it is a state to be cultivated, not just a greeting. Then the warning against being misled by anyone pointing outward — do not look over here, do not look over there. Why? Because *the Son of Humanity exists within you*. This is the *bar enasha*, the human one, present as an interior reality. It is Luke 17:21 in different wording, and Thomas 3, and Thomas 113. The whole gospel of Jesus in one line — the kingdom, the Christ, the son of the human, is within.

title: Where the Mind Is
pullquote: The mind is what sees. Not the eyes, not the flesh — the faculty between soul and spirit that turns toward the treasure and beholds it.
core_message: You see spiritual reality with the mind that stands between soul and spirit, and where that mind is fixed, there your treasure lies.

primary.jesus_words: "You're blessed because you didn't waver at the sight of me. For where the mind is, there is the treasure." (To Mary's vision query:) "They don't see in the soul or in the spirit, but the mind which exists between the two is what sees the vision."

context: Mary Magdalene has just told the disciples that the risen teacher appeared to her in a vision. Peter and Andrew scoff. But in the fragment that survives, Jesus first blesses Mary for not wavering at the sight of him and gives the reason: where the mind is, there is the treasure. It is the same principle Jesus states in the Sermon on the Mount — where your treasure is, there your heart will be — turned around and sharpened. What you fix your mind on is what you have. Attention is possession. If your mind is fixed on the kingdom, you are in the kingdom. If it is fixed on lack, grievance, or fear, that is your treasure and that is where you live.

title: My Power, My Power
pullquote: The Gospel of Peter's cry from the cross — not "my God" but "my power" — the divine strength within, spoken of as departing at the moment of death.
core_message: In the Gospel of Peter's cross scene, Jesus calls out to the divine power within him as it withdraws at the moment of death.

primary.jesus_words: "My power, O power, thou hast forsaken me!"

context: The Gospel of Peter is a second-century passion narrative, known only in a fragment found at Akhmim in Egypt in 1886, and quoted by Bishop Serapion around 190 AD before he pulled it from his church for its unorthodox flavor. In its crucifixion scene, the cry from the cross is not the Psalm 22 line the canonical gospels give — *Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani* — but a different sentence: my power, O power, thou hast forsaken me. Then, the text says, he was taken up. The wording matters. Peter is not reporting the Aramaic of Psalm 22. He is describing an inward event — the *dynamis*, the divine power that had rested on Jesus through his ministry, departing at the moment of death.

title: I Come to Abolish Sacrifices
pullquote: "I am come to do away with sacrifices."
core_message: Jesus came to end the sacrificial system, not to complete it with his own blood.

primary.jesus_words: I am come to do away with sacrifices, and if you cease not sacrificing, the wrath of God will not cease from you.

context: This is the sentence the Jesus Way keeps returning to, preserved outside the canon by the Ebionim — the poor ones, the community that traced its lineage through James the brother of Jesus and never left Jerusalem. Epiphanius quotes it in the 370s while attacking them, which is exactly why it survived: he needed to prove they were heretics for saying it. *I have come to do away with sacrifices, and if you cease not sacrificing, the wrath of God will not cease from you.* No sacrificial theology. No blood atonement. No lamb required. The Temple's whole economy — priest, altar, animal, blood, receipt — is what Jesus came to end. And the community closest to him in blood and geography preserved that teaching against every incentive to soften it.
